summary:
Edo State stands under Nigeria's national legal framework. Its own documented record is one of mob violence against people accused of same-sex conduct, and it contains no instance in which police protected the person accused.

In February 2008, in a remote community in Edo State, police declared Ugbogbo Ovbukhan wanted over 'gay practice' after he and his partner Jerry were found together. A mob beat both men for desecrating the community; Ovbukhan escaped before police arrived and police arrested Jerry for interrogation. The Nigerian Observer reported the wanted declaration on 15 August 2008.

On 10 June 2010, The Nigerian Observer reported from Benin City, in Oredo local government area, that Mark Osato Edomwonyi narrowly escaped being killed by a mob after he was found with his partner Paddy in Paddy's rented apartment. A neighbour raised the alarm; Edomwonyi fled through the backyard before the mob arrived, and the crowd then, in the newspaper's words, 'unleashed terror' on Paddy. No police intervention, arrest or prosecution appears in the report, and Edomwonyi's whereabouts were still unknown when it was filed.

In May 2018, at Ekpoma, a mob lynched one of two men found together while the other escaped. The report presented the killing as an 'abominable act' against traditional heritage, treating it as community redress.

For a visitor, the documented exposure in Edo comes from community perception rather than from a prosecution: in these accounts it is neighbours, not patrols, who raise the alarm, and the single police action documented across the three cases was taken against the couple rather than against those who beat them. The cases reported involve men accused of same-sex conduct, and the inventory holds no Edo case in which a report identifies the victim of violence as a transgender person. Risk to a trans visitor therefore has to be read from the way accusations of sexual and gender nonconformity mobilise a crowd, not from a documented attack on a trans person in the state.
tangentialFactors:
The 2018 Ekpoma killing was reported under a traditional-heritage framing, with the attack presented as a response to an 'abominable act'. Violence that is locally legible as community redress shapes whether it is reported and whether it is investigated as a crime.

The documented incidents are separated by a decade and by geography. They occurred in Benin City in Oredo local government area, in Ekpoma, and in a remote community in the state, so the record does not tie the exposure to a single locality or to urban Edo alone.

The 2008 file is unusual in the record for producing formal police action, but that action ran against the accused: a wanted declaration for one man and the detention of the other for interrogation, with no step taken against the crowd that had beaten them.
localsOnly:
In the recorded cases the alarm came from neighbours and community members rather than from officials, and discovery happened in private or residential settings: a couple found together in a remote community in 2008, and a rented apartment in Benin City in 2010.

Residents accused in these circumstances have no example of protection in the record. The 2008 case ended with one man beaten and fleeing and his partner held for interrogation. The 2010 case ended with one man escaping the neighbourhood and the other left to the crowd, with no arrest or prosecution recorded. The 2018 case at Ekpoma ended with one man dead.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Initiative for Equal Rights' 2024 Human Rights Violations Report, published in January 2025, records 556 violations affecting 850 victims based on real or perceived SOGIESC across Nigeria. The figures are national and carry no Edo-specific breakdown, and the organisation states they represent only a fraction of the true scale, so no Edo rate or magnitude can be derived from them.

No general homicide or violence rate for Edo State appears in the source inventory, so the count of documented incidents in the state cannot be compared against the level of background violence there.

The outcome for Paddy after the 2010 attack is not recorded, nor is the outcome of Jerry's 2008 detention or the disposition of the wanted declaration against Ugbogbo Ovbukhan. No prosecution of any mob is documented in the 2008, 2010 or 2018 cases.

The three incidents rest on reports by a single local newspaper, The Nigerian Observer. Incidents reported through other channels, or not reported at all, would not appear in this record.
